title: EUCLEAK Side-Channel Attack on the YubiKey 5 Series (Revealing and Breaking Infineon ECDSA Implementation on the Way)
abstract: The present work unearths a side-channel vulnerability in the cryptographic library of Infineon Technologies, one of the most important secure element manufacturers. This vulnerability-that went unnoticed for 14 years and about 80 highest-level Common Criteria certification evaluations-is due to a non constant-time modular inversion. The attack requires physical access to the secure element (few local electromagnetic side-channel acquisitions, i.e. few minutes, are enough) in order to extract an ECDSA secret key. The attack is demonstrated on a FIDO hardware token from Yubico where it allows to create a clone of the FIDO device. Yubico acknowledged that all YubiKey 5 Series (with firmware version below 5.7) are impacted by the attack. Furthermore, strong arguments tend to indicate that all Infineon security microcontrollers (including TPMs) that run the Infineon cryptographic library are vulnerable to the attack. 4026 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

The present work unearths a side-channel vulner- ability in the cryptographic library of Infineon Technologies, one of the most important secure element manufacturers. This vulnerability - that went unnoticed for 14 years and about 80 highest-level Common Criteria certification evaluations - is due to a non constant-time modular inversion. The attack requires physical access to the secure element (few local electromagnetic side-channel acquisitions, i.e. few minutes, are enough) in order to extract an ECDSA secret key. The attack is demonstrated on a FIDO hardware token from Yubico where it allows to create a clone of the FIDO device. Yubico acknowledged that all YubiKey 5 Series (with firmware version below 5.7) are impacted by the attack. Furthermore, strong arguments tend to indicate that all Infi- neon security microcontrollers (including TPMs) that run the Infineon cryptographic library are vulnerable to the attack. 1. Introduction Secure elements are the root of trust of secure systems. These small microcontrollers should be able to generate, store and manipulate secrets while ensuring their full con- fidentiality and integrity. And they must be able to do so even when it falls into the adversary's hands. The most stringent certification scheme of security de- vices is under the umbrella of Common Criteria (CC for short) and was preliminary designed for smart cards eval- uation 1. This evaluation, organized around certification bodies (public institutions from the signatory countries of the SOGIS), is executed by an independent and accred- ited ITSEF laboratory. These evaluations are tedious and extremely time-consuming, especially when aiming at the highest security level: AVA_VAN_5 2. Integrated in a public key infrastructure, secure elements allow - with unparalleled security guarantees - to safely authenticate a genuine product ( e.g. for access control) or validate that a piece of software was not modified ( e.g. 1. https://www.commoncriteriaportal.org/files/ppfiles/ssvgpp01.pdf 2. The Vulnerability Assessment Number , it goes from 1 to 5. The CC EAL level aggregates, among other things, the AVA_VAN_X level for boot purpose). Secure elements are then everywhere, from the Trusted Platform Modules (TPM for short) that can be found managing the secure boot of most computers (personal or server), to the banking, travel or ID cards. They are also omnipresent in high-end smartphones (notably for payment purpose), in cars and more generally in any IoT device that requires (or advertises) high level of security. Notably, in the last decade, secure elements made their way inside two new kind of products: crypto-currency hardware wallets and Fast Identity Online (FIDO for short) hardware tokens. Both of these products claim high level of security while being easily in the hand of an adversary. While undergoing the most thorough security evaluations from highly skilled ITSEF laboratories, few vulnerabilities have been found in certified secure elements in the past by independent security researchers. The ROCA attack [1], the TPM-Fail attack [2] and A Side Journey to Titan [3], [4] are certainly the most important ones in recent years. The present work unveils a new side-channel vulnerability in the ECDSA implementation of Infineon Technologies on any security microcontroller family of the manufacturer. This vulnerability lies in the ECDSA ephemeral key (or nonce) modular inversion, and, more precisely, in the Infineon implementation of the Extended Euclidean Algorithm (EEA for short). The exploitation of this vulnerability is demonstrated through realistic experiments on a YubiKey 5Ci (a FIDO hardware token from Yubico). The side-channel acquisition requires physical access to the device and an electromagnetic probe to capture ECDSA execution side-channel traces (see the acquisition setup in Section 1.3). The adversary only needs to have access to the Infineon chip for few minutes. The offline phase of the attack took about 24 hours; with more engineering work in the attack development, it would take less than one hour. All YubiKey 5 Series - before the firmware update 5.7 released during our responsible disclosure - are affected by the attack. Concretely, the attack on a YubiKey requires that the attacker steals the hardware token (as well as the 4026 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00219 PIN, or any biometrics, if enabled) and acquires several EM side-channel traces for each web account before giving back the device to its legitimate user. The attacker will then be able to extract the ECDSA private key associated to each protected web account and create a clone of the YubiKey for these accounts. Investigating two more recent chips from Infineon, it seems that all products relying on the ECDSA of Infineon cryptographic library and running on an Infineon security microcontroller are affected by the attack. As a matter of fact, all recent Infineon security microcontrollers and TPMs have seen their CC certificates replaced during the couple of months following the vulnerability disclosure. We then estimate that the vulnerability exists for more than 14 years in Infineon top secure chips. These chips and the vulnerable part of the cryptographic library went through about 80 CC certification evaluations of level AVA_VAN_4 (for TPMs) or AVA_VAN_5 (for the others) from 2010 to 2024. A coordinated responsible disclosure has been conducted with Infineon - naturally including Yubico and Feitian, as well as the German (BSI) and French (ANSSI) certification bodies. It started on April the 19th 2024 and Infineon confirmed (July 26th, 2024) that they implemented and tested a patch to their library, eliminating the attack threat. A full write-up of the attack was released publicly on September 3rd 2024 [5], [6]. Related Works on Binary EEA. To our knowledge, this is the first time an implementation of the EEA is shown to be vulnerable to side-channel analysis. However, a large literature considers side-channel attacks on the binary versions of the EEA (more popular than the classical EEA for efficiency reasons). In the seminal work of Acıic ¸mez et al. [7], the authors show that an attacker being able to recover the exact sequence of if-then-else branches taken in a binary EEA execution ( e.g. using side-channel analysis), can recover the modular inversion inputs. This attack has applications in both RSA and ECDSA and many cryptolibraries were subsequently found vulnerable to various adaptations of this attack [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13]. While most works consider that the attacker has access to noiseless information, this is not always the case in practice (e.g. in case of a blinding countermeasure). Recently, Kwong et al. [13] introduced a powerful attack algorithm able to recover the inversion inputs with a single execution of the binary EEA (i.e. a single sequence of branches taken by the binary EEA) that can cope with some specific errors (some erasures are accepted for some specific branches). While this attack is specific to the practical case that the authors face, it shows that dealing with noisy side-channel traces is sometimes manageable. The important literature on side-channel attacks on the binary EEA makes the use of the classical EEA appealing to developers. Indeed, as the Infineon implementation discovered in our work, it is possible to implement the EEA completely avoiding branches, hence removing any obvious source of leakage. More pragmatically, as stated in [11], there is no published attack on the EEA and then one can consider this algorithm as safe. Our Contribution. • The reverse-engineering of Infineon EEA implemen- tation fully based on the study of the ECDSA side- channel traces captured on a Feitian open JavaCard smartcard (where the ECDSA private key can be freely chosen); • The design of a new generic and robust ( i.e. it can accept some errors) side-channel attack process against the EEA; • The practical demonstration of the full attack on a YubiKey 5Ci where the ECDSA private key is initially unknown; • The identification and study of the two main other families of Infineon secure elements indicating that the vulnerability is certainly present in all versions of Infineon cryptographic library. Paper Organization. Necessary information about FIDO protocol, ECDSA and the side-channel acquisition chain are presented in the remainder of this introduction. Sec- tion 2 presents a first side-channel reverse engineering of the ECDSA implementation, and more particularly of the nonce modular inversion, leading to the identification of a sensitive leakage. Section 3 introduces a new generic and flexible side-channel attack on the Extended Euclidean Algorithm while Section 4 will take us deeper in the reverse- engineering of Infineon implementation to uncover addi- tional sensitive leakages. The successful application of the attack on Feitian A22 and YubiKey 5Ci products is described in Section 5. In Section 6, the identification of the main families of Infineon security microcontrollers leads to select and test two more recent chips (namely the Optiga Trust M and Optiga TPM ). The results indicate that the vulnerability is also present on these chips. Finally, Section 7 concludes with a simple mitigation solution that Infineon chose to follow and several directions of research opened by this work. 1.1. FIDO Hardware Tokens FIDO Hardware tokens are USB and/or NFC (sometimes Bluetooth) authentication devices for web services that support FIDO protocol 3 (e.g. a Google account). This authentication factor can be added to a traditional login/password authentication (in that case our attack requires that the attacker also knows the login/password of the target, e.g. using phishing) or as a unique factor of authentication (as specified in the FIDO2 protocol and 3.
